title: Why Generative AI Will Underperform Expectations in Education
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Dan Meyer tries to build shared context with AI technologists who think chatbots will be world-class tutors for every child. He says he is not arguing that AI will be bad for schools, only that it will not transform education in the next five years, cost teachers their jobs or be preferred over human tutors. His central claim is that students come to school to answer two questions, 'Who am I?' and 'How do I do this?', and for most K-12 students those are the same question. A chatbot can address the second but cannot answer the first, so each minute with a chatbot is a minute not spent learning who you are in relation to others. He allows that the picture changes for older, post-secondary students whose identities are more settled, and he adds reader responses and further hype quotes as updates.
points: Meyer separates 'AI might help some students' from the far bolder claim that AI tutors will transform schooling or replace teachers.
Students attend school to answer 'Who am I?' and 'How do I do this?', and in K-12 these questions are entangled.
Asking a teacher or peer a math question also tells a child how others value their ideas, which a chatbot cannot supply.
The argument is age-dependent: post-secondary students with firmer identities may value chatbots more.
Technologists misjudge schooling and teachers misjudge AI, so progress needs shared context rather than heat.
quotes: My counterparts know much about AI technology and little about schools. I know much about schools and little about AI technology.
I’m not trying to explain why AI will be bad for education, rather why AI will not transform education inside of the next five years, and I’d guess much longer.
If you want to understand why AI will fail to transform education, all you need to understand is that, for most K-12 students, those two questions are the same question.

Every minute students spend with a chatbot is a minute not getting an answer to one of the two questions they came to school to answer. Whenever students learn "how do I do this?" with another person, they are getting answers to both.

This is not uniformly true across all students, of course. As kids get older and turn into adults, their identities become less and less pliable. They can separate the study of a new idea from the study of self. Students will appreciate AI chatbots more in post-secondary spaces, for example, where their identities are better defined and where their next best alternative to the chatbot—a 500-person lecture hall where you are anonymous to your instructor and classmates—doesn’t do much to answer “Who am I?” anyway.

The main liability of teachers in conversations like these is that they don’t understand AI technologies all that well. The main liability of AI technologists is that they don’t understand all that well how important the question “Who am I?” is to school learning and how hard it is for most students to separate that question from the kinds of questions that AI chatbots seem pretty good at answering. Hope this helps.
